taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes older literature treated it as conspecific with S. hammondii and that northern and southern populations of the western spadefoot are genetically distinct.
fieldMarks: Gray, brown, tan or greenish with dark spots or small blotches on the back and upper legs; faint light stripes occasionally on the back and sides.
Red-tipped tubercles scattered over the back, head and upper surfaces of the legs; large eyes; short spade-shaped tubercle on the underside of each hind foot.
Unlike the plains spadefoot, it has no bony boss between the eyes; it is reported to smell like peanuts when handled.
behavior: Active at night, usually during humid or wet periods of spring and summer (late March-September in northern Texas).
Emerges after heavy rain; breeding choruses last 1-2 days and eggs hatch in about 2 days; ponds often dry before metamorphosis.
Burrows underground or uses rodent burrows when inactive; migrates between breeding pools and non-breeding terrestrial habitat.
Tadpoles occur as a carnivorous morph (mainly fairy shrimp) and an omnivorous morph that eats more detritus and algae.
habitat: Desert grassland, shortgrass plains, creosote bush, sagebrush and semi-desert shrubland, mixed grassland-chaparral, pinyon-juniper and pine-oak woodland and open pine forest; breeds in temporary pools formed by heavy rain.
range: Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado and northern Oklahoma south through Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to Mexico (Guerrero and Oaxaca); up to about 2,470 m. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Plains spadefoot (Spea bombifrons)
lookalikes.howToTell: Has a hard bony boss between the eyes and does not smell of peanuts; its call is a brief snore, faster than the Mexican spadefoot's long stuttering snore.
